title: The Leeds office
text: Morning all. I'll keep this short because you've probably heard it in the kitchen already. The Leeds office is being made {{redundant|redundant}} at the end of March. I'm not {{at liberty|at liberty}} to share the numbers yet, and before anyone asks, no, I don't know who leaked it to the group chat. Everyone affected will get a proper one-to-one with me next week, not a two-minute Teams call. I'd rather we got through this without it turning into a punch-up. Kettle's on if you want to talk. Dan

gloss.leaked: told people something that was supposed to stay secret
gloss.one-to-one: a private meeting between two people
gloss.kettle's on: a British way of saying 'come and have a cup of tea'

title: Gran's flat
text:
Mum: Did you get to Gran's?
Sam: Yeah. She looked proper {{frail|frail}} today, Mum. Both hands on the kettle.
Mum: She's eighty-nine, love. Was the flat {{damp|damp}} again?
Sam: Worse. Black patches on the bedroom wall and that smell. Landlord came out with some {{feeble|feeble}} excuse about the gutters.
Mum: Don't start, petal. I'll ring him Monday and I won't be polite.
Sam: Can I listen in?
Mum: No.

gloss.gutters: the channels on a roof edge that carry rainwater away
gloss.petal: an affectionate name for someone, like 'love'
gloss.landlord: the person who owns the flat you rent

title: Below the ridge
text: Below the ridge, a fox waits in the {{dense|dense}} bracken. It is a hunter by instinct and a {{scavenger|scavenger}} by necessity, because winter up here is long and the rabbits have had the sense to stay underground. A red kite has already found what the fox is after: a sheep that fell in the night. The kite eats first. That is the rule on the hill. The fox will get its turn, but not before the crows have had theirs.

gloss.ridge: a long narrow top of a hill
gloss.bracken: a tall fern that covers hillsides
gloss.kite: a large bird of prey with a forked tail

title: Two brothers and a will
text: Her third film is the one that shuts the doubters up. Two brothers come back to a farmhouse in Cumbria to sort out their mother's will, and an old {{enmity|enmity}} wakes up with them before the kettle's even boiled. The only warmth comes from an {{amiable|amiable}} vicar who keeps turning up with casseroles nobody asked for. Shame about the score, which tells you what to feel ten seconds before the actors do. Still. Four stars, and I'd watch it again.

gloss.shuts the doubters up: proves wrong the people who didn't believe in her
gloss.will: a legal document saying who gets your things when you die
gloss.vicar: a priest in the Church of England
gloss.casseroles: meals cooked slowly in one dish in the oven
gloss.score: the music written for a film

title: Question seven
text:
"Question seven. Which Latin word meaning 'at the back' is also a polite way of saying your bottom?"
"{{Posterior|posterior}}!" Dave shouted, before the host had finished reading.
"Thank you, Dave. Three pints in and not a single {{inhibition|inhibition}} left."
"It's a cracking quiz, this," Dave said, dead pleased with himself.
"It would be," said his wife, "if you'd let the rest of us answer one."

gloss.three pints in: after drinking three pints of beer

title: The jar from Dorset
text: The {{specimen|specimen}} came up from Dorset in a jar of cloudy spirit, a beetle no bigger than a grain of rice. Marcus wiped the bench with a {{damp|damp}} cloth, laid out his tools, and then sat and looked at the thing for twenty minutes without touching it. "First one found in Britain since 1911," he said when I asked. "I'm not going to rush it just because you want your lunch."

gloss.spirit: strong alcohol used to preserve specimens
gloss.grain: one small piece of rice or sand
gloss.bench: a long work table in a lab or workshop

title: The drawer of shame
text: Every kitchen has one drawer that won't shut. Mine holds a {{redundant|redundant}} {{utensil|utensil}} for every job: three peelers, a garlic press that has never crushed a clove in its life, and an avocado slicer, which is a spoon with ambitions. This weekend I emptied the lot onto the table and was honest with myself. I kept the wooden spoon my gran used, handle worn pale, and binned the rest. The drawer shuts now. I feel like a different person.

gloss.peelers: tools for removing the skin of vegetables
gloss.clove: one piece of a garlic bulb
gloss.worn: damaged or smooth from long use
gloss.binned: threw away (British: put in the bin)

title: Rovers 0, City 5
text: City {{obliterated|obliterate}} Rovers on a night when the fog was so {{dense|dense}} that the far goal was a rumour for most of the first half. The home defence was all over the place from the first minute, and by the fourth goal the fans had stopped singing and started heading for the car park. Their manager, clearly fuming, refused to blame the weather. "Fog was the same at both ends," he said. "Only one team could see the ball."

gloss.rumour: a story people tell that may not be true
gloss.blame: to say someone is responsible for something bad

title: First date, Peckham
text: He was {{amiable|amiable}} enough, in the way estate agents are, and for the first hour Priya was polite. Then the second gin turned up and her {{inhibitions|inhibition}} left with the first one. She told him about the flat with the mouldy bathroom, the ex, the cat that hated her. He laughed in the right places. He admitted he'd never finished a book, which should have been a deal-breaker, and somehow wasn't. She found, slightly to her horror, that she fancied a third gin.

gloss.estate agents: people who sell or rent out houses
gloss.gin: a clear strong alcoholic drink, usually with tonic
gloss.mouldy: covered in mould, the green or black growth in damp places
gloss.deal-breaker: a problem that would stop you going ahead

title: Notice to tenants
text: Dear Resident, following the survey of the rear wall of Block C, the council now accepts that the {{damp|damp}} is structural and not, as previously suggested, caused by residents drying washing indoors. We apologise for that suggestion. Repairs begin in June. We are not yet {{at liberty|at liberty}} to name the contractor. We know many of you have had a rotten two years with the housing office, and we hope this letter is a start.

gloss.survey: a careful inspection of a building to check its condition
gloss.structural: to do with the walls and frame of a building
gloss.contractor: a company hired to do building work
gloss.housing office: the council department that manages rented homes

title: The flower stall
text:
"They're a bit past it, these," the woman said, poking the roses.
"They're fine," said the lad on the stall. "One {{petal|petal}} comes off and suddenly it's a crime scene."
"I'm paying eight quid."
"You're paying eight quid for roses that were in Holland on Tuesday. Have the tulips, they're {{diminutive|diminutive}} but they'll last the week."
She took the tulips. She also took the roses, because it was Mother's Day and she'd left it till the last minute, as usual.

gloss.past it: too old to be any good (informal)
gloss.lad: a young man or boy (British informal)
gloss.stall: a small open-air shop, often at a market
gloss.left it till the last minute: waited until the latest possible time

title: The hyena thing
text: Right, so your nan's fine, but the vet bill for the dog is not. Turns out he's been eating something dead down by the canal. Vet said he's basically a {{scavenger|scavenger}} with a collar on. Also she said the thing you found in the garden last week was almost certainly {{carrion|carrion}} a fox had left, so stop poking stuff with sticks. Dinner's at seven. Bring the good wine, not the stuff from the garage.

gloss.basically: more or less, in simple terms
gloss.the garage: here: the petrol station shop, which sells cheap wine

title: Bonfire night, early
text:
Dad: Fire {{broke out|break out}} in Keith's shed about an hour ago.
Me: WHAT. Is he ok??
Dad: He's fine, he's stood in the garden in his dressing gown directing the firemen. The shed's gone. Mower's gone. The hose he tried first was so {{feeble|feeble}} it barely reached the fence.
Me: Was it the heater again?
Dad: He says a fox knocked it over. The fireman's face said otherwise.
Me: Tell him I'll bring round a bottle tomorrow.
Dad: Bring two. One's for the fireman.

gloss.dressing gown: a loose coat you wear over pyjamas at home
gloss.knocked it over: pushed it so that it fell

title: Full time at the Crown
text: It was a {{dense|dense}} crowd for a Tuesday, three deep at the bar and the telly turned up far too loud. The penalty went in, somebody's pint went over, and that was that. Fighting {{broke out|break out}} by the fruit machine, two blokes who had clearly been waiting all evening for an excuse. Maureen, who has run the Crown for thirty years, didn't even put her glass down. "Out," she said, not loudly. They went. Then she turned the telly up again.

gloss.fruit machine: a gambling machine in a pub (British)
gloss.put her glass down: stop drinking to deal with something

title: Letter from the school
text: Dear parents and carers, chickenpox has {{broken out|break out}} in Year 2, with six cases confirmed since Monday. If your child comes out in spots, please keep them at home until the spots have scabbed over, which usually takes five days. Mrs Okafor, our ever {{amiable|amiable}} school nurse, is on hand all week if you have questions, and has asked us to pass on that calamine lotion and cut fingernails will save everyone a lot of scratching. The Harvest Festival will go ahead as planned. Kind regards, Mr Patel, Headteacher

gloss.carers: people who look after a child but are not the parents
gloss.scabbed over: formed a hard dry cover over a wound
gloss.pass on: tell someone something you were told
